en: Then, having gathered the collection of necessary materials and being accompanied by highly skilled assistants, at an auspicious lunar day and planetary conjunction during the forenoon, the practitioner—possessing the sciences, having established the connection with the deity of the Cakreśa, and having performed prior service—should construct a maṇḍala-hall in the northeastern direction of a city, town, village, grove, or monastery, wherever his mind finds delight.

Then, having gathered all necessary requisites and being accompanied by a most trustworthy companion, one should perform the preliminary service (*puraścaraṇa*) through the yoga of the deity Cakreśvara, together with the consort, at an auspicious time during the morning, such as when the virtuous factors (*kuśaladharma*) are present.
In a village, a city, a market town, a park, a monastery, or a house—whichever direction is sovereign or wherever it is pleasing to the mind—one should construct the maṇḍala hall.

If the mandala is performed in the eastern direction, there will be the death of the king and various calamities for the people. In the southern direction, he for whose sake the mandala is made will die. In the western direction, the preceptor [will die]. In the northern direction, he who has entered it [will die]. In the southeastern direction, there will be rain. In the southwestern direction, famine. In the northwestern direction, wind and rain. Near a natural element-caitya, there will be death. Near water presided over by nāgas, there will be water.

Knowing that the child’s death would occur in the shade of a tree, he abandoned everything, selected an excellent circular area sloping toward the northeast, and there, having prepared a mandala with fragrant substances and the like, worshipped the deities of the mandala, offered a *bali* sacrifice, and dismissed them into the sky; then, he honored the local guardians (*kṣetrapāla*) and others dwelling there with offerings of *bali* and other gifts.

If a mandala is constructed in the eastern direction, the lord of the land will die, and various harms will befall the people. In the southern direction, whoever intended the mandala for will die; in the west, the preceptor; in the north, those who have entered it; in the southeast, rain; in the southwest, famine; and in the northwest, a windstorm.

Having understood that one dies near a stūpa containing the relics of the Buddha’s disciples, that water arises near a place where *nāgas* dwell, and that children die in the shade of trees, one should completely abandon all such places. Then, having carefully examined a site for a most auspicious mandala that slopes toward the east and north, one should construct a maṇḍala there with fragrant substances and the like.

Having properly worshipped the deities of the mandala and offered the *bali* oblation, one should elevate it into the sky. There, one should worship the field-protectors (*kṣetrapāla*) and others residing there with the *bali* and offerings, [reciting]:

"Ye 'tra santi surā nāgā yakṣā rakṣāṃsi cāpare | yāce 'haṃ tāṃ bhuvaṃ te ca maṇḍalārthaṃ sṛjanti mām ||" (Those who are here—gods, nāgas, yakṣas, and other rākṣasas—I entreat you for this ground; may they grant me the site for the sake of the mandala.)
Whatever gods, nāgas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, or others who dwell here, I shall now take possession of this ground; for the sake of the maṇḍala, please grant it to me.

Having thus entreated three times, and having ascertained that the [permission] has been granted by them through a dream or otherwise and is not prohibited, one should—in the forenoon of the following day—pray to Śrī Vajradhara and the others situated in the expanse of the sky, and cause them to grant mental authorization. At midday, having dispelled the obstacles either through the meditation on the protection wheel and the nailing down of obstructors (*vighnakīlana*) or by means of a wrathful fire-offering (*krūrahoma*), and in the case of the fire-offering, having performed a pacifying fire-offering (*śāntikahoma*) in the afternoon in the hearth located in the southeast direction for the sake of protecting the disciple, one should [empower] that ground with: *oṃ āḥ vighnāntakṛt hūṃ*.

Having sprinkled [the site] with mustard seeds, water, and ashes while reciting this *sarvakṛt* mantra, and having meditated there upon the Earth Goddess (*pṛthivīdevatā*) possessing the previously described characteristics while seated in the vajra-paryaṅka posture, one should first offer the worship of water for the feet, water for sipping, and the *argha* offering; then, having entreated her with the three subsequent verses, and once she has replied, "Let it be done so," one should mentally raise her up and establish her in the sky.

Thus one should make this supplication three times. Having ascertained whether permission has been granted or denied in dreams and so forth, one should mentally supplicate Śrīvajradhara and the others residing in the center of the sky during the forenoon of another day and request their authorization. Then, at midday, one should either meditate on the protection wheel and the ritual staking of obstructors, or—

One should expel obstructing spirits through a wrathful fire offering (*hom*). For the sake of protecting the disciple, one should also perform a peaceful fire offering in the evening into a hearth situated in the direction of the fire offering. Furthermore, that ground should be purified with mustard seeds, water, and ashes over which the *sarvakarmika* mantra—*oṃ āḥ vighnāntakṛta hūṃ*—has been recited.

Assuming the vajra posture, one should visualize the Earth Goddess with the characteristics that will be described. Preceded by the offering of water for the feet, water for the face, the arghya-water, and general offerings, one should make supplication three times with the verse beginning "O Goddess, you... as it is recited.
Then, having mentally lifted her up while she utters the words "So be it," one should request her to remain in the sky.

Considering the ground situated there to be free from obstacles, and having offered a *bali* offering as before, one should have a pit dug—measuring either the depth of a neck (*kaṇṭha*), a fathom (*vyāyāma*), or reaching the water or the bedrock—at the chest of the *vāstu-nāga*, according to the distinction of inferior, middling, or superior accomplishments; or it may measure the depth of a knee, a hip, or a navel. This is the procedure for digging the earth.

Then, having ascertained that the ground is free from obstacles, one should offer the *bali* and, as before, dig into the shoulder-blade area of the local deity or *nāga*—reaching as far as the neck or the lips, or until it collapses—according to the distinction between inferior, middling, and supreme accomplishments, [digging] down to the level of the knees, the hips, or the navel.

Then, since stones, bones, hair, charcoal, and so forth are harmful, one should remove all such things; having filled the pit with that very same earth moistened with fragrant water, and if there is a deficiency, having added more earth and sprinkled it with scented water consecrated by the *amṛtakuṇḍalin* mantra while reciting the syllable *HŪṂ*, one should construct a level ground—either sixteen cubits or twelve cubits in measure, and four cubits high—and mark it out using the method for laying the lines (*sūtra*) as will be described hereafter.

Then, having removed all defective elements such as stones, bones, hair, and charcoal, one should sprinkle that very ground with fragrant water; it should be filled in the pit, or if it is not full, it should be filled with other materials.

One should sprinkle it with water scented by reciting the mantra of Amṛtakuṇḍalī, and then strike the ground. On a level site measuring sixteen cubits—or alternatively twelve cubits—and having a height of half a cubit, one should lay out the lines according to the ritual for laying lines that will be explained.

In the center of that, one should fashion a moon-seat (*candrāsana*) twelve or eight cubits in circumference, one span (*vitasti*) in height, with a slightly raised middle and sloping toward the east and north; beneath it, one should make a lotus-base (*mekhalā*) measuring eight finger-breadths in width, four finger-breadths in height, shaped like a lotus petal and complete with filaments.

In its center, there is a circular moon seat measuring twelve or eight cubits, possessing a height of one span, which is slightly elevated in the middle and slopes toward the east and north. Below that, one should fashion a girdle in the form of lotus petals together with filaments, having a width of eight finger-breadths and a height of four finger-breadths.
Having laid out four lines for a square measuring twenty-four cubits,
with a mandala of twelve cubits at the end of the garland of rays, one should again lay out four lines after setting aside four cubits from each of those sides.

Starting from the northeast direction, one should proceed in order along the cord to place twenty pillars on the altar platform and twelve pillars above it; having placed a corner-pediment upon the four pediments, one should set down four small corner-pillars and provide the four corner-sections together with their pedestals.

Alternatively, one should have a mandala-hall constructed in another manner, well-proportioned, free from defects such as being jagged, equipped with eight parts and four gates, adorned with water-pots (kalaśas), furnished with eight banners in the colors of the world-protectors (dikpālas), topped with a white victory banner, beautified by plantain pillars, decorated with four archways made of sacrificial wood, and graced within by a canopy of moonlight, as well as by garlands, chowries, and other ornaments.

Starting from the direction of Īśāna, there are pillars at the twenty-four lines; there are twelve pillars on the pedestal. Above that are the four roofs; having constructed the four-cornered roof, one should place four small pillars and set four beams reaching to the ends of the corners.

Whether according to his own or another's tradition, it should be made free from defects such as frayed edges and well-constructed; it should possess the four gates of the eight branches, be endowed with a *bhadraghaṭa* (auspicious vase), and bear victory banners (*dhvaja*) the color of the world-protectors (*lokapāla*), with a white *vijaya-dhvaja* (victory banner) upon its crown, beautified by a plantain tree pillar.

One should construct a maṇḍala pavilion adorned with the four gates fashioned from species of sacrificial wood, beautified at its perimeter by a moon-shaped parasol, and decorated with garlands, yak-tail whisks, and other ornaments.
Alternatively:
Then again,
if one is unable to extract all the faults of the thorns.
Having placed his hand [upon it], he should recite the mantra; that indeed is the greatest purification.
In places such as palaces, stone surfaces, cow-pens, hermitages, and monasteries, or on the banks of rivers,
purification occurs even without digging, provided the site was previously consecrated.

If all those defects cannot be removed, one should touch [the site] with the hand and recite the mantra; that itself is the great purification. Whether it be a fine mansion, a mountain peak, a cow-pen, a temple, or a riverside—provided these sites have been prepared beforehand, they are pure even if not physically dug up.

Therefore, one should transform this earth—which has been dug, scraped, and prepared—into space while reciting "Oṃ bhūḥ khaṃ. Then, having visualized it as consisting of vajras by means of the mantra "Hūṃ laṃ hūṃ," one should consecrate the ground by placing the hand upon it while reciting these three mantras: "Oṃ medini vajrībhava vajrabandha hūṃ; Oṃ hana hana vajrakrodha hūṃ phaṭ; Oṃ āḥ hūṃ śodhaya śodhaya rakṣa rakṣa hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ."

Therefore, for these grounds and for those that have been excavated or struck, one should transform them into space by reciting *oṃ bhūkhaṃ*. Then, one should meditate upon them as being of the nature of vajra by means of this: *hūṃ laṃ*. [Then recite: *oṃ medini vajrabhāva bandha hūṃ / oṃ hana hana vajrakrodha hūṃ phaṭ / oṃ āḥ hūṃ śodhaya śodhaya rakṣa rakṣa hūṃ*.
Having recited this mantra, one should touch the ground with the hand and consecrate it.

Upon that ground—which has been smeared with scented water consecrated with that same mantra and whose center contains five jewels, medicinal herbs, and grains consecrated with *kuṇḍalī*—one should visualize the terrestrial deities residing in the sky as being present within it. Reciting "Oṃ Āḥ Hūṃ," one should perform the lotus-turning gesture (*kamalāvarta*) and recite the hundred-syllable mantra.

In its center, having placed as appropriate the five kinds of jewels, medicines, and grains that have been consecrated with mantras, and having sprinkled it with scented water consecrated with mantras, one should offer the *bali* and foot-washing water and so forth to the Earth Goddess (*pṛthivī-devī*) abiding in space, and then dissolve her [into the site]. Reciting "OṂ ĀḤ HŪṂ" and performing the lotus-circumambulation (*padakora*), one should recite the hundred-syllable mantra.

Through the firm conviction that the entire universe has the single flavor of emptiness, one should resolve upon the stage whose intrinsic nature is perfectly pure suchness; thus is the unsurpassed purity.

Through the superior conviction that "the manifold is emptiness and of one taste," one should resolve that the ground is of the nature of suchness, which is utterly pure; this is the unsurpassed purity, and thus concludes the procedure for the mandala house and so forth.
Thus concludes the ritual for the mandala hall and so forth.
